title: Self Crossing
description:
# Self Crossing

You are given an array of positive integers `distance`.

You start at `(0, 0)` on the Cartesian plane. Move `distance[0]` meters north, then `distance[1]` meters west, then `distance[2]` meters south, then `distance[3]` meters east, and continue rotating counter-clockwise after every segment.

Return `true` if any non-adjacent part of the path intersects a part drawn earlier. Touching an old endpoint also counts as crossing. Return `false` if the path never touches or crosses itself.

## Example 1:

**Input:** distance = [2,1,1,2]
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** The fourth segment crosses the first segment at `(0, 1)`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** distance = [1,2,3,4]
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** Every segment keeps the spiral expanding outward.

## Example 3:

**Input:** distance = [1,1,1,2,1]
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** The path contracts far enough to touch a point that was already visited.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= distance.length <= 10^5`
*   `1 <= distance[i] <= 10^5`

solutions.name: Three Local Crossing Cases
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan each segment from the fourth one onward. In a counter-clockwise spiral, a new segment can only create a first crossing with the segment three, four, or five steps before it. Test those three local patterns directly.

## Key Insight

Before the first crossing, all earlier segments form either an expanding spiral or a just-started contraction. That geometry rules out every older segment except the three local ancestors, so the formula is complete rather than a heuristic.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each distance is checked once.
- Space Complexity: O(1), because the detector only reads a constant number of previous lengths.

solutions.name: Segment History Geometry
solutions.description:
## Approach

Materialize every segment as an axis-aligned line with two endpoints. For the current segment, test intersection only against the non-adjacent segments at offsets three through five; those are exactly the possible first-collision ancestors in this spiral.

## Key Insight

This version turns the algebraic cases back into geometry. It is useful when teaching why endpoint touches, collinear overlaps, and perpendicular crossings all count, because all three reduce to rectangle interval overlap.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each segment is compared with at most three earlier segments.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the code stores all segment endpoints for clarity.

solutions.name: Six-Segment Ring Buffer
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep only the last six drawn segments in a ring buffer. Each new segment is checked against the three non-adjacent ancestors that can still matter, then it overwrites the oldest segment slot.

## Key Insight

The path has a fixed left-turn order, so a first crossing cannot jump past the five most recent segments. This keeps the geometric implementation while removing the full segment history.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because every segment performs a constant number of intersection tests.
- Space Complexity: O(1), because the ring buffer has a fixed size.

solutions.name: Expanding Then Contracting State
solutions.description:
## Approach

First skip the strictly expanding prefix. At the first non-expanding segment, normalize the previous side if the path can touch the old boundary, then require the remaining suffix to keep strictly contracting. Any later failure means self-crossing.

## Key Insight

A valid non-crossing spiral has one shape transition: outward growth followed by inward contraction. The transition adjustment accounts for the special endpoint-touch cases that a plain expanding/contracting comparison would miss.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because the expanding and contracting scans are linear.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because this implementation copies `distance` before using one entry as the transition boundary. It can be made O(1) by mutating the input array.

solutions.name: Reverse Path Local Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Reverse the distance list and run the same local crossing detector from the other end of the drawn path. Reversing does not change whether the geometric path intersects itself, only the order in which the segments are visited.

## Key Insight

Self-crossing is symmetric under reversing traversal. This gives a useful cross-check of the local-case proof and helps students separate the geometry from the chosen starting direction.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because the array is reversed once and scanned once.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the reversed distance array is stored explicitly.
